section.title: Ministry Begins in Galilee
section.sectionRationale: With John imprisoned, Jesus settles in Capernaum and launches His public ministry in Galilee, the region Isaiah foretold would see a great light. He takes up John's message of the kingdom, calls His first disciples from their nets, and moves through Galilee teaching, preaching, and healing, drawing enormous crowds. The section shows the dawn of the kingdom in word and deed.
section.thesis: The light Isaiah promised dawns as Jesus preaches the nearness of the kingdom in darkened Galilee, summons ordinary fishermen to leave everything and follow Him, and demonstrates the kingdom's arrival by healing every kind of sickness, so that the reign of God is announced and displayed together.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Jesus withdraws to Galilee, fulfilling Isaiah's light in the land of Zebulun and Naphtali; He begins to preach the kingdom; He calls the first four disciples; and He teaches, preaches, and heals throughout the region as crowds gather.

units.label: A light in Galilee
units.note: the land of the shadow of death

verses.text: When Jesus heard that John had been imprisoned, He withdrew to Galilee.
Leaving Nazareth, He went and lived in Capernaum, which is by the sea in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali,
to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah:
“Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the Way of the Sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles,
the people living in darkness have seen a great {{phos|light}}; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned.”
From that time on Jesus began to preach, “{{metanoeo|Repent}}, for the kingdom of heaven is near.”
As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, He saw two brothers, Simon called Peter and his brother Andrew. They were casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.
“Come, {{akoloutheo|follow}} Me,” Jesus said, “and I will make you fishers of men.”
And at once they left their nets and followed Him.
Going on from there, He saw two other brothers, James son of Zebedee and his brother John. They were in a boat with their father Zebedee, mending their nets. Jesus called them,
and immediately they left the boat and their father and followed Him.
Jesus went throughout Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the {{euangelion|gospel}} of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness among the people.

News about Him spread all over Syria, and people brought to Him all who were ill with various diseases, those suffering acute pain, the demon-possessed, those having seizures, and the paralyzed, and He healed them.
Large crowds followed Him, having come from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan.

phos.gloss: Light. Isaiah promised that the darkened, half-Gentile north would see a great light; Matthew declares that light dawns in the ministry of Jesus, who elsewhere calls Himself the light of the world, John 8:12.

metanoeo.gloss: To change one's mind, turn around, repent. Jesus opens His ministry with the same summons as John, a decisive turning toward God demanded by the arrival of His reign.

akoloutheo.gloss: To follow, come after, accompany as a disciple. More than walking behind, it means attaching one's whole life to Jesus as Master; the fishermen leave nets and family to follow, the pattern of all discipleship.

euangelion.gloss: Good news, glad tidings, the announcement of a King's saving reign. The gospel of the kingdom is the good news that God's promised rule has arrived in Jesus, proclaimed and displayed in His teaching, preaching, and healing.

basic.context: When John is arrested, Jesus moves north and makes Capernaum, a lakeside town in Galilee, His base. Matthew sees this as fulfilling Isaiah's promise that a great light would dawn on that darkened, half-Gentile region. Jesus begins to preach the same message as John, calls two pairs of fishermen brothers to follow Him, and travels Galilee teaching, announcing the kingdom, and healing every kind of sickness, until crowds pour in from every direction.
basic.hermeneutics: This section is a summary of the launch of Jesus' ministry, showing its shape: word and deed together. Notice that the kingdom is both proclaimed, in preaching and teaching, and demonstrated, in healing. Notice too the immediate, whole-life response of the first disciples, which Matthew holds up as the model of what following Jesus means.
basic.originalLanguages: The light Isaiah foretold has come. Jesus calls people to repent, to turn around, because the kingdom has arrived. He calls the fishermen to follow, to attach their whole lives to Him as disciples, and they do. And He proclaims the gospel of the kingdom, the good news that God's saving reign has drawn near in Him.
basic.typology: The light dawning in Galilee of the Gentiles hints that this King will be a light not only to Israel but to the nations. The calling of fishermen to become fishers of men echoes God gathering a people, and the healings signal the arrival of the age when the blind see and the lame walk, the marks of the promised kingdom.
basic.christ: Jesus is the great light shining in the darkness, the King whose reign is dawning. He calls disciples with sovereign authority, and they leave everything to follow. His teaching and healing reveal Him as the one who both announces and brings the kingdom of God, the fulfillment of Israel's hope.
basic.god: God keeps His promise to shine light on a people in darkness. His reign draws near not in a palace but in a Galilean town, among ordinary people and their ordinary troubles. He heals the sick and gathers the outcast, showing that His kingdom means the undoing of the curse and the mending of a broken world.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 9:1-2 is the prophecy of light in Galilee that Matthew quotes. Mark 1 and Luke 5 give parallel accounts of the calling of the fishermen. Isaiah 35 pictures the healings that mark the coming of God. And Matthew 9:35 repeats this summary of teaching, preaching, and healing.
basic.oneStory: The King has come, and His reign begins to break into the world. In a despised northern region, the light long promised finally dawns; ordinary people are called into His service; and sickness and darkness begin to flee at His approach. The kingdom of heaven is not merely announced but is visibly arriving, and its first ambassadors are fishermen who left their nets to follow the light of the world.

context.literary:
Matthew 4:12 to 25 is the hinge between the preparation of Jesus and the teaching of Jesus. Three scenes of preparation (the genealogy and birth, the baptism, the temptation) lead here, and the Sermon on the Mount follows. The section itself falls into four movements: the move north with its Isaiah quotation, verses 12 to 16; the one-line summary of His message, verse 17; the calling of two pairs of brothers, verses 18 to 22; and a summary of teaching, preaching and healing, verses 23 to 25.

The words 'From that time on Jesus began to preach' in verse 17 are a signal. Matthew uses the same phrase only once more, in Matthew 16:21, 'From that time on Jesus began to show His disciples that He must go to Jerusalem and suffer.' Many readers see these two statements as the markers of the Gospel's two main halves: first the proclamation of the kingdom, then the road to the cross.

Verse 23 and Matthew 9:35 are nearly identical, 'teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness.' They bracket chapters 5 to 9, so that the Sermon on the Mount (the teaching and preaching) and the miracle stories of chapters 8 and 9 (the healing) are set out as the content of one ministry. Matthew gives the words first and then the deeds, and presents the whole as the work of the Messiah.

Notice also the movement of the verbs. In the first scene Jesus is the one who hears and withdraws; in the call scenes He sees and calls; in the summary He is surrounded and acts on behalf of crowds. The passage moves from retreat to company, from one man in Capernaum to a crowd from five regions.
context.historical:
Galilee was the northern part of the land, a region of fertile hills, farming villages and the busy shore of the Sea of Galilee, which Luke calls the Lake of Gennesaret, Luke 5:1, and John the Sea of Tiberias, John 6:1. In Jesus' day it was ruled by Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great. John the Baptist had denounced Antipas, and that is why he was imprisoned. When Matthew says Jesus 'withdrew' it is the same verb he uses for retreats from danger, as when Joseph withdrew to Galilee in Matthew 2:22 and when Jesus withdrew on hearing of John's death in Matthew 14:13.

Capernaum, a lakeside town on the northwest shore, was a place of trade, a customs point, and a base of fishing families. Fishing was a real industry: boats, nets and hired workers, and fish were sold and preserved for sale. Zebedee has a boat and his sons work with him, Matthew 4:21, so these men were not poor drifters. When they leave, they leave a livelihood and a family business.

Isaiah's words speak of a region with a sorrowful history. Zebulun and Naphtali were the first tribal lands to fall to Assyria, when Tiglath-pileser took 'Galilee, including all the land of Naphtali,' 2 Kings 15:29. Over the following centuries the area received a mixed population and was called 'Galilee of the nations,' Isaiah 9:1. Pious Jews in Judea looked down on it. By the time of Jesus, the 'Way of the Sea,' the main road from the coast, ran through it.

Crowds in verse 25 come from Galilee, the Decapolis (ten largely Gentile cities east of the Jordan), Jerusalem, Judea and the far side of the Jordan, and the news reaches Syria. The listing reads like a map of the whole land, with Gentile regions included.
context.canonical:
The Isaiah passage Matthew quotes sits at the start of one of the Bible's great messianic chapters. Isaiah 9:1-2 promises light to the lands the Assyrians first devastated, and the verses that follow explain why: 'For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given,' who will reign 'on the throne of David,' Isaiah 9:6-7. Matthew quotes the opening and leaves the rest for the reader to remember. The light arrives in the person of the promised king.

The theme of light runs through Scripture. At creation God said, 'Let there be light,' Genesis 1:3, and Paul says the same God has made His light shine 'in the face of Jesus Christ,' 2 Corinthians 4:6. Zechariah sings that the Dawn will visit 'those who live in darkness and in the shadow of death,' Luke 1:79, using the words that Matthew quotes. Simeon calls the child 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles,' Luke 2:32, and Jesus says of Himself, 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12. Isaiah 49:6 had already promised that the Servant would be a light for the nations.

The call of the fishermen has its own roots. The prophets used the image of fishing for the gathering of people, Jeremiah 16:16, and Ezekiel pictured fishermen standing along a restored river, Ezekiel 47:10. The Gospels record the same event: Mark 1:16-20, Luke 5:1-11, and John 1:35-42, which tells of earlier contact with Jesus.

The healings are taken up elsewhere in Matthew. After a day of exorcisms and cures, Matthew says this fulfilled 'He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases,' Matthew 8:17, quoting Isaiah 53. Later Jesus answers John with the same signs, 'The blind receive sight, the lame walk,' Matthew 11:5, which echo Isaiah 35:5-6.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wanted his readers to see that the ministry of Jesus did not begin by accident or by a flash of popularity. It began in a particular place, at a particular time, as the fulfilment of a promise, and with a particular message. He ties the first public word of Jesus to the last word of John, 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near,' Matthew 3:2, so that Jesus carries on from John, only more fully.

He also wanted to settle what following Jesus means. The fishermen are not asked to hold an opinion; they are asked to leave a boat and a father and to go after Him. There is no explanation, no trial period, no list of benefits. The call itself and the one who gives it are the reasons. Matthew's readers, many of whom had paid a price to follow Jesus, were meant to find themselves in these men.

A third aim is to show the kingdom as a fact and not only an idea. The summary of Jesus' work in verses 23 to 25 shows what the nearness of the kingdom looks like in practice: instruction in the synagogues, the good news announced, bodies and minds healed, and people flocking in from everywhere. For readers in Matthew's time, who may have been wondering whether the kingdom had really come, the summary was an answer.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is a narrative summary, and its details are descriptive. The record that Jesus moved to Capernaum, that He called four fishermen and that He healed every sickness is not a command to relocate, to become a fisherman, or to expect a healing in the same way. These are things that happened in the unique period when the Messiah announced His kingdom.

What does carry over is the shape of the call and the substance of the message. 'Repent' remains the first word of the gospel, and 'follow Me' remains the call of Jesus to everyone who hears Him. We should not read the sudden departure of the fishermen as a rule that everyone must walk away from their work, since Jesus does not ask this of everyone; the Gospels also show people He sent home, such as the man from the Gerasenes in Mark 5:19. What we are meant to learn is that nothing, whether a trade, a family or a plan, may stand above Jesus' call.

The healings need similar care. They are signs that the kingdom has arrived, and Christians may and should pray for the sick and care for them, but the passage does not promise that every illness will be healed now. It shows what the King can do and what the final kingdom will be.

debates.question: What does it mean to become fishers of men?

views.label: A call to gather people into the kingdom
views.case: Jesus turns the disciples' trade into their mission: as they once drew fish from the sea, they will now draw men and women into God's saving reign through the gospel.

views.label: An echo of prophetic gathering and judgment
views.case: The Old Testament uses fishing imagery for gathering the nations and for judgment, Jeremiah 16:16 and Habakkuk 1:15; the phrase may carry the weight of God assembling a people at the end of the age.

debates.bearing: Either way the disciples are commissioned to bring people to Jesus; their whole calling is now defined by His mission, not their old trade.

debates.question: How could the fishermen leave everything at once to follow Jesus?

views.label: A prior acquaintance now brought to decision
views.case: John's Gospel records earlier contact between Jesus and these men, so Matthew's scene captures the decisive moment of a call they were already prepared to answer.

views.label: The sovereign, compelling authority of Jesus' call
views.case: Matthew stresses the sheer power of the summons: Jesus speaks, and at once they leave nets and father, showing that His word creates the obedience it commands.

debates.bearing: Both honor the reality that following Jesus is a response to His authoritative call and involves leaving other loyalties behind to attach oneself wholly to Him.

debates.question: How does Matthew's 'fulfillment' of Isaiah 9:1-2 work?

views.label: A direct, predicted fulfilment
views.case: Isaiah promised that the lands that were humbled would be honoured, and the Messiah's ministry begins exactly there. Matthew presents the geography of Jesus' work as a deliberate keeping of God's word, so that even the starting place was foretold.

views.label: A pattern of promise and fulfilment in history
views.case: Isaiah spoke first about relief from the Assyrian gloom of his own day, and the pattern of God lighting up a darkened people finds its final instance in Jesus. Matthew sees in Jesus the full answer to what the earlier deliverance only began.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that Matthew is showing Jesus as the one in whom the words reach their goal. The choice of Galilee tells the reader that the Messiah has come to the overlooked, not to the centre of power.

study.originalLanguages:
Matthew's 'From that time on' in verse 17 is apo tote, a phrase that marks a new stage. It is joined to the verb 'began,' erxato, and then to 'preach,' kerysso, which means to announce publicly as a herald. This is the word for a royal messenger's proclamation. Jesus does not offer a lecture; He makes an announcement.

The message itself is 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.' The verb for 'is near,' engiken, is in the perfect tense, so it means the kingdom has come close and now stands at hand. 'Kingdom of heaven' is Matthew's characteristic phrase and uses 'heaven' respectfully in place of the name of God. It does not mean a place in the sky; it means God's own reign.

In the quotation of Isaiah, the people 'living in darkness' are in Greek those who are sitting in darkness, a word that suggests settled helplessness. The light is said to have 'dawned,' aneteilen, the verb used for the rising of the sun. The word 'light' stands at both ends of the couplet, seen by the people in one line and dawning on them in the next. 'The shadow of death' is a phrase from the Old Testament, as in Psalm 107:10, where it describes the plight of prisoners in affliction.

The call in verse 19 is 'Come, follow Me.' The Greek is literally 'Come after Me,' deute opiso mou, an invitation to walk behind a master. In Jewish custom students usually chose their teacher; here the Teacher chooses. The promise 'I will make you fishers of men' uses the verb 'make,' poieo, and shows that the change is something Jesus will bring about, not something the disciples achieve. The word for 'at once,' euthys, is used in both verse 20 and verse 22, though the BSB renders it 'immediately' in the second, and Matthew repeats it to stress the speed of the response.

In verse 21 the brothers are 'mending' their nets. The Greek verb is katartizo, which means to put in order, to restore, to make ready. It is a quiet detail: they are preparing for the next day's work when Jesus calls them.

The summary in verse 23 distinguishes 'disease,' nosos, from 'sickness,' malakia. Together with 'every' repeated, the pair is meant to sound complete. In verse 24 one group is described by a word that literally means 'moonstruck,' selēniazomenous, which the BSB renders 'those having seizures.' The ancient world associated certain disorders with the moon, but Matthew uses the word simply as a category of sufferers, set apart from the demon-possessed. The verb for healing, therapeuo, can mean to serve or attend to, and so it hints at care as well as cure.

typology.type: Light dawning on Galilee of the nations
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah's darkness over Zebulun and Naphtali was literal: the Assyrian armies had taken the first of Israel's tribal lands, 2 Kings 15:29. The light that arrives in Jesus is both a rescue from that history and a larger light, the same one that Genesis 1:3 called into being at creation. He says of Himself, 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12, and then calls His followers the light of the world as well, Matthew 5:14. The type points beyond Israel, since Simeon names Him 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles,' Luke 2:32. It falls short only as a political picture; the darkness lifted is the darkness of sin and death, not merely foreign rule.

Jeremiah 16:16 speaks of God sending 'many fishermen' to catch His scattered people, and Ezekiel pictures fishermen along a river of life, Ezekiel 47:10. In Matthew 4:19 the image is turned to a calling: the men who haul fish will be made to gather men and women into the kingdom. The commission grows into the Great Commission, 'make disciples of all nations,' Matthew 28:19. The escalation is that the net now reaches every nation. The type is imperfect in one respect: fish are caught and die, while those caught by the gospel are drawn out of death into life.

When Elijah threw his cloak over Elisha, Elisha asked to kiss his parents goodbye first, and Elijah allowed it, 1 Kings 19:19-21. Jesus' call is more demanding: Simon and Andrew leave their nets, and James and John leave their boat and their father. Jesus later says that no one who puts a hand to the plow and then looks back is fit for the kingdom, Luke 9:62. The pattern of a prophet calling a worker from labour is carried up to its highest point. Jesus is no new prophet with a mantle but the One whose own word makes disciples, and the type falls short because it can only point to a call.

typology.type: The signs of the age to come
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 35:5-6 promised a day when the eyes of the blind would be opened, the lame would leap, and streams would break out in the desert. Matthew's healings are the first of these signs. Jesus later tells John's messengers that 'the blind receive sight, the lame walk,' Matthew 11:5. Matthew also quotes Isaiah 53, 'He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases,' in Matthew 8:17, linking His healings to His suffering. The healings are foretastes, not the whole: the people He healed would sicken again and die, and the end of sickness awaits the new creation.

study.christ:
Matthew's first picture of the adult Jesus in His ministry is of a light. The people were 'sitting in darkness,' and He is the dawn that rises on them. This is not light that He reflects; it is light that He is, as He says in John 8:12. Everything in the passage serves that claim: the move to Galilee fulfils prophecy, the call comes with a sovereign word, and the cures follow His own command.

He is the herald and the substance of the message. The announcement 'the kingdom of heaven is near' is made by the one who brings it, so that the message can be summed up as the nearness of a person. In Matthew 12:28 He says, 'if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.' The healings are not bonus acts of kindness; they are the reign of God in action.

He is the sovereign caller. The fishermen do not volunteer, and Jesus does not ask for their qualifications. He sees them, speaks, and they come. The only parallel in the Old Testament is the way God summoned prophets, and Jesus does it with His own authority. Peter's later confession, 'we have left everything to follow You,' Matthew 19:27, shows that the call cost something. Yet the promise, 'I will make you,' shows that He supplies what the disciples lack. The men Acts later describes as 'unschooled, ordinary men' had the one qualification that mattered, that 'they had been with Jesus,' Acts 4:13.

He is the compassionate healer. The gathering of all kinds of sufferers shows that no case lies outside His reach: pain, seizures, paralysis, demonic oppression. Matthew will later tell us the reason, that He 'took on our infirmities,' Matthew 8:17. The word for His work here is a visible sign of a deeper work. The one who removes sickness in Galilee will bear the curse behind it at Jerusalem.

He is also a Saviour for more than Israel. He goes to a region called 'of the nations,' and the news reaches Syria and the Decapolis. This is a hint of what Matthew will state fully later, that the King of the Jews is a light for the nations. Yet Matthew is careful about timing: Jesus says in Matthew 15:24 that He was sent first to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. The light begins in Israel's neglected corner and then spreads.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The fishing image is not a hidden allegory in which every detail of nets and boats stands for something; the New Testament uses it for the disciples' mission, not as a code. And we should not read the immediacy of the fishermen as if they understood fully who He was. Their understanding grew slowly. What the passage sets before us is the one who calls and the call that cannot be put off.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who keeps promises across centuries. Isaiah spoke of a light for Zebulun and Naphtali around seven hundred years before Matthew, and the Gospel says the light came to exactly that region. The way Matthew points to a specific place shows that the promises are not vague hopes but words God carries out in history, down to the geography. When God says He will honour what He humbled, Isaiah 9:1, He does it.

It shows a God who goes to the dark places. Galilee was the place Jerusalem thought of as second class, a land mixed with foreigners and long marked by defeat. God does not wait for the centre to be ready; He begins in the margin. Psalm 107 describes those who 'sat in darkness and in the shadow of death' and whom God 'brought out,' Psalm 107:10 and 14, and the Galilean ministry is that rescue carried out in person. The God of the Bible has always had a habit of beginning where people least expect.

It shows a God whose rule comes near. The kingdom 'is near,' and the nearness is real because it has a face and a voice. God's reign is not reached by a long climb; it comes to a lakeside town. There He heals, teaches and calls. This is the God who 'inhabits eternity' and also dwells 'with the oppressed and humble in spirit,' Isaiah 57:15.

It shows a God who calls and equips. His summons does not depend on the strength of those called. The gospel gives the order: 'Come, follow Me, and I will make you.' God supplies both the invitation and the transformation, and He uses ordinary people for work only He can accomplish.

It shows the pairing of word and deed in God's character. He speaks and He acts; He teaches and He heals. The nearness of the kingdom is announced and visible. That unity runs through Scripture, from the creation by speech to the exodus, to the incarnation.

It shows God's compassion as well as His power. In the next chapters we are told that Jesus saw the crowds and 'was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd,' Matthew 9:36. The healing hand of Matthew 4 is the hand of a shepherd.

For worship, this passage invites us to praise a God who keeps His word to the letter, who goes looking in unlikely places, and who still calls people by name. It also asks us a question about our response. Light that has dawned should be walked in; a call that has been heard should be answered.

crossReferences.note: The prophecy Matthew quotes. Isaiah speaks of the northern tribal lands, once humbled by invasion, being honoured, and of a people in darkness seeing a great light. The verses that follow, Isaiah 9:6-7, name the child and king who brings it, so Matthew's quotation hints at the whole promise of a Davidic ruler.

Records the first blow against the north: Tiglath-pileser of Assyria captured Galilee and Naphtali and took the people into exile. This explains why Isaiah's darkness was so literal, and why Matthew's report that light has come to this exact region is a story about God reversing an old wound.

Mark's account of the same events puts the arrest of John, the proclamation of the gospel, and the call of the same four fishermen in nearly the same order. It shows that Matthew is not the only witness to the pattern of preaching, then calling, and helps us see what is common to all the accounts.

Luke tells of the call of Simon, James and John in the setting of a miraculous catch of fish. It adds that Simon fell at Jesus' knees and said, 'Go away from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.' It complements Matthew's brief report by showing what lay behind the fishermen's readiness to leave everything.

John records an earlier meeting. Two disciples of John the Baptist followed Jesus and spent a day with Him, and Andrew brought his brother Simon. This helps explain how fishermen could respond so quickly in Matthew 4, since they had already met Him.

God says He will send for 'many fishermen' to catch His people, and afterward 'many hunters.' The image of fishing for a people has an Old Testament background of gathering, though it is mixed with judgment. Jesus' call gives the image a clear, gracious direction: the fishing is to bring people into the kingdom.

Isaiah promises that the eyes of the blind will be opened, the deaf will hear and the lame will leap. Matthew 4:23-24 is a first fulfilment of this picture, and Matthew 11:5 makes the connection explicit when Jesus names these same signs as the answer to John's doubt.

The summary of Matthew 4:23 is repeated almost word for word, with the addition that Jesus has compassion on the crowds and asks His disciples to pray for workers for the harvest. Together the two summaries frame the Sermon on the Mount and the miracles, and show that the call of the Twelve grows out of the need of the crowds.

Jesus sends out the Twelve, including the four from this scene, with the same message, 'The kingdom of heaven is near,' and the same authority to heal. The fishermen who were called to follow become those who go out, so that the work of verse 23 becomes theirs as well.

Zechariah's song speaks of the Dawn visiting 'those who live in darkness and in the shadow of death,' using the very words of Isaiah that Matthew quotes. Luke applies the prophecy at the birth of Jesus, and Matthew applies it as His ministry begins, showing that the whole Gospel tradition read Isaiah 9 as pointing to Him.

The rulers marvelled at the boldness of Peter and John, 'unschooled, ordinary men,' and realised they had 'been with Jesus.' It shows the long result of this call: the fishermen who followed became witnesses whose confidence came from their time with Him.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story starts with light spoken into darkness, Genesis 1:3, and then moves into a world where light is overcome. Humanity falls, the nations scatter, and Israel is herself carried off, beginning with the tribes of the north, 2 Kings 15:29. The prophets promise that this will not be the last word. Isaiah looks past the darkness to a child, a son and a king on David's throne. Matthew 4 is where that promise begins to be kept.

The first thing the King does is to go to the place the darkness fell hardest. That is typical of the whole story: God's rescue begins at the margins, with a shepherd boy, a barren woman and a conquered land. The second thing He does is to gather people. The Old Testament story of God calling one man, Abram, and one nation is now carried forward by the calling of four men beside a lake. They will become the apostles, and through them the offer of the kingdom goes out to all nations, as Matthew 28:19 says.

The healings join the passage to the larger story as signs. Isaiah had promised that when God came, the blind would see and the lame leap. What Isaiah saw in the distance is now seen in Capernaum. But these signs are limited: they help some of the sick and hold back death only for a time. They are the first drops of a rain that will fall in full in the new creation.

Looking back, the passage answers the question of Genesis 3, what has become of the light? Looking forward, it prepares for the Sermon on the Mount, where the King describes the life of His kingdom, and for Matthew 16:21, where the same King sets out to suffer. The light has come, and the way of the cross will show what it costs.

The story ends with a city that 'has no need of the sun or moon' because 'the glory of God illuminates it, and the Lamb is its lamp,' Revelation 21:23. The people who once sat in darkness will walk in His light for ever, and the fishers' catch will be a multitude from every nation.

quiz.q: Why does Matthew say Jesus settled in Galilee, in Zebulun and Naphtali?

options.text: To fulfill Isaiah's prophecy that a great light would dawn on that darkened region.
options.note: Verses 14-16 tie the move to Isaiah 9:1-2 and the promised light.

options.text: Because Galilee was safer than Judea after John's arrest.
options.note: He did withdraw after John's arrest, but Matthew's stated reason is the fulfillment of Isaiah.

options.text: Because Capernaum was His and His family's hometown.
options.note: He left Nazareth for Capernaum; the emphasis is on fulfilling prophecy, not returning home.

options.text: Because the temple leaders had invited Him to teach there.
options.note: No such invitation is mentioned; the move fulfills Isaiah's promise of light.

quiz.q: What message did Jesus begin to preach?

options.text: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.
options.note: Verse 17 gives His opening message, the same as John's.

options.text: Follow Me and I will make you fishers of men.
options.note: That was His call to the disciples, not the summary of His preaching, which was repentance and the kingdom.

options.text: The law must be kept perfectly to enter the kingdom.
options.note: His message was repentance because the kingdom had drawn near, not perfect law-keeping.

options.text: The temple in Jerusalem would soon be destroyed.
options.note: That comes much later; here He preaches repentance and the nearness of the kingdom.

quiz.q: How did Simon, Andrew, James, and John respond to Jesus' call?

options.text: At once they left their nets, and even their father, and followed Him.
options.note: Verses 20 and 22 stress their immediate, costly response.

options.text: They agreed to follow Him after the fishing season ended.
options.note: The text stresses immediacy; they left at once, not after a delay.

options.text: They followed but kept working as fishermen on the side.
options.note: They left their nets and boat to follow; the point is a clean break.

options.text: They asked for time to consider and later declined.
options.note: The opposite; they followed immediately.

quiz.q: What three things characterized Jesus' ministry throughout Galilee?

options.text: Teaching in the synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing the sick.
options.note: Verse 23 names all three, showing the kingdom announced and displayed.

options.text: Preaching and healing, but not formal teaching.
options.note: He also taught in the synagogues; the summary names teaching, preaching, and healing together.

options.text: Debating the Pharisees and cleansing the temple.
options.note: Those come later; here the ministry is teaching, preaching, and healing.

options.text: Training the twelve in private, away from crowds.
options.note: He ministered publicly to crowds, teaching, preaching, and healing.

quiz.q: What does the healing ministry reveal about the kingdom Jesus brings?

options.text: That God's reign means the undoing of sickness and the mending of a broken world.
options.note: The healings are signs that the promised kingdom, when the sick are made whole, has arrived.

options.text: That Jesus mainly came to relieve physical suffering.
options.note: Healing displays the kingdom, but His mission centers on the gospel of the kingdom and, ultimately, the cross.

options.text: That only the sick could enter the kingdom.
options.note: The healings are signs of the kingdom's arrival, not a rule about who may enter.

options.text: That the kingdom is purely spiritual with no effect on the body.
options.note: The bodily healings show the kingdom touches the whole person and the created world.

questions: The first disciples left their nets and their father at once to follow Jesus. What might following Jesus wholeheartedly cost you, and what are you still holding back?
Jesus turned fishermen into fishers of men. How is Jesus calling you to use your ordinary work, skills, and relationships for His mission?
The light dawned in a despised, dark region, not in a place of power. Where do you need to trust that God works in the overlooked and unlikely corners of your life?
Jesus both announced the kingdom and demonstrated it in mercy to the suffering. How can your witness to Christ join words of good news with deeds of compassion?
Crowds came to Jesus from every direction with every kind of need. What need are you bringing to Him today, trusting Him to meet you?

translationNotes.note: Galilee of the Gentiles leads into the following verse; together they quote Isaiah 9:1-2.
The land of the shadow of death renders a vivid Hebrew phrase for deep darkness; Matthew applies Isaiah's promise of light to the coming of Jesus.
The Decapolis, noted in the source as the Ten Cities, was a league of Gentile-influenced cities east of the Jordan, showing the wide reach of Jesus' fame.
